title: The Dzumsa of Lachung and Lachen
meta_description: How Lachung and Lachen govern themselves through the Dzumsa, a village assembly led by an elected Pipon, recognised in Sikkim's panchayat law since 1982.
summary: Lachung and Lachen are run by the Dzumsa, a village assembly of every household, led by an elected headman called the Pipon and two assistants. Sikkim's panchayat law has recognised it since 1982, and the 1995 amendment treats both Dzumsas as Gram Panchayats. Its rules shape your visit, from plastic to dams.

sections.heading: A council older than the road
paras: Most villages in India elect a panchayat. Lachung and Lachen, the two highest villages on the North Sikkim tourist circuit, do something older. They govern themselves through the Dzumsa, a word usually explained as a meeting place or assembly of the people. Every household sends a member, decisions are taken together, and the village is led by a headman called the Pipon.

The people of the two valleys are known as Lachungpa and Lachenpa, Bhutia communities who for generations moved between winter homes in the villages and summer pastures higher up, with yaks, sheep and a little barley, potato and buckwheat. A scattered, seasonal life on a cold frontier needed a way to share pastures, settle disputes and organise work, and the Dzumsa grew to do that. Its exact age is not well documented; written accounts describe it as several centuries old, and the short Wikipedia article on the Dzumsa places its formal shape in the 19th century.
What makes it remarkable is not only that it survives, but that the modern state chose to work through it rather than replace it.

sections.heading: Who does what
paras: The structure is simple. The details below come from published accounts, including a North Bengal University study and a 2024 Mongabay India article on Lachung by Shrishtee Bajpai, and practice differs slightly between the two villages.
Lachen and Lachung each have their own Dzumsa, and each sets its own rules; what applies in one valley does not automatically apply in the other.

sections.heading: How a Pipon is chosen
paras: Traditionally, the Pipon was chosen by the adult representatives of each family for a term of one year, and the Pipon then named two Gyapons to help. Later accounts show the rules shifting with time. According to the 2024 Mongabay India piece, in Lachung the Pipons are now selected from two different parts of the village in December, by the Tibetan calendar, and serve for two years. A Pipon there is expected to be over 45, to know the village well, and to understand its customs.

That last condition matters. The Pipon is not simply an administrator; he is meant to hold the village's memory. He knows which family grazes which pasture, which grove is sacred, how a dispute was settled twenty years ago. In a place where many rules have never been written down, that knowledge is the law.

sections.heading: A council for a herding life
paras: Much of the Dzumsa's work has always been about land held in common. High pastures, forests for firewood and timber, and grazing routes for yaks and sheep belong to the village as a whole, not to single families. The Dzumsa decides when herds move up to summer pastures and when they come down, who may cut wood where, and what fine is due when someone breaks the rule. In a cold valley where a lost season of grazing can mean a hard winter, those decisions matter to every household.

The council also organises shared work and village rituals. Repairs to paths and bridges, preparations for festivals at the monastery and help for a family after a death have traditionally been arranged through the Dzumsa, with each household expected to contribute labour or money. Visitors sometimes see the results without knowing it: a newly cleared path, prayer flags raised along a ridge, or a lodge that is closed for a day because its owners are at a village gathering.

sections.heading: Recognised by Sikkim's law
paras: When Sikkim brought in its own panchayat law after joining India in 1975, Lachen and Lachung could have been folded into the standard system. Instead, the Sikkim Panchayat Act of 1982 protected their traditional councils and recognised the annual election of the Pipons. The Sikkim Panchayat (Amendment) Act of 1995 went further: it declared that the Dzumsas existing in the two villages for many centuries shall be deemed to be Gram Panchayats.

In practice, that gives the Dzumsa two kinds of authority at once. It exercises the powers of a Gram Panchayat under state law, including development funds and schemes, and it keeps the powers it already held under customary law. Very few village bodies in India have that double standing, and it explains why rules in Lachung and Lachen can differ from those in Mangan or Gangtok.

sections.heading: The decisions visitors notice
paras: You will not attend a Dzumsa meeting, but you will meet its decisions. The best known is about dams. According to the Mongabay India article, after three years of agitation the Dzumsa of Lachung decided in 2009 to ban any hydropower project on its rivers, and even proposing one in public is treated as an offence in the village. In a state where hydropower has reshaped many valleys, the Lachung Chu still runs free.

Other decisions touch tourists more directly. The local bodies in Lachung and Lachen have at times restricted packaged plastic water bottles, so carry a refillable bottle. Rules on rubbish, on where vehicles may park, and on what happens at sacred groves and springs come from the village too. Rules change from season to season, so check current status before you travel and follow what your driver or lodge tells you.
list: Carry a refillable bottle; packaged water may be restricted.
Take your rubbish back to Gangtok; bins are few.
Ask before you photograph people, prayer flags being raised, or the inside of the monastery.
Do not pick plants, break rhododendron branches or disturb yaks in the pastures.
Keep noise down in the village after dark; lodges serve dinner by 8 pm and the village sleeps early.

sections.heading: Why it matters for the future
paras: The October 2023 Teesta flood, triggered by the burst of South Lhonak Lake, cut Lachen off for 887 days and damaged roads to Lachung too. For two tourist seasons, the villages had almost no visitors. The Dzumsa was the body that organised local responses, spoke for the villages to the district, and decided how tourism would restart.

As tourism returns, the Dzumsa faces new questions: how many lodges a village of a few hundred households can support, how to share income between lodge owners and herders, and how to keep young people in a place where winters are long. Its answers will shape what you find when you visit. If you stay in a locally owned lodge, eat local food and pay fairly, your money goes into exactly the community that governs the valley.

sections.heading: Sources and further reading
paras: For the legal position, see the Sikkim Panchayat (Amendment) Act, 1995, and the Sikkim Panchayat Act, 1982, both summarised in public law databases and in the Comptroller and Auditor General's reports on local bodies in Sikkim. For Lachung today, read Shrishtee Bajpai's 2024 Mongabay India article, republished by Vikalp Sangam as Living territory of Lachung, and the related Kalpavriksh commentary. The Wikipedia article on the Dzumsa is a short starting point. Ask your Lachung or Lachen host too, and treat what you hear as their village's own account.

faqs.a: The Dzumsa is the traditional self-governing assembly of Lachung and Lachen in North Sikkim. Every household sends a member, and the assembly is led by an elected headman called the Pipon, helped by two Gyapons. It settles disputes, manages common resources such as pastures and forests, and sets village rules that visitors also follow.

The Pipon is the elected headman of the Dzumsa in Lachung or Lachen. He chairs meetings, settles disputes and represents the village to officials. Traditionally the term was one year; according to a 2024 Mongabay India article, Lachung now selects its Pipons in December for two years, and expects them to be over 45 and well versed in custom.

faqs.q: Is the Dzumsa recognised by law?
faqs.a: Yes. The Sikkim Panchayat Act of 1982 protected the Dzumsas of Lachen and Lachung, and the Sikkim Panchayat (Amendment) Act of 1995 declared that they shall be deemed to be Gram Panchayats. They exercise panchayat powers under state law alongside their customary powers, an unusual double standing in India.

Yes, in small ways. Village rules on plastic water bottles, rubbish, parking and behaviour at sacred sites come from the local bodies. Packaged water has been restricted at times, so carry a refillable bottle. Your driver and lodge will tell you the current rules; follow them, because they are the village's own law.

faqs.q: Why are there no dams on the Lachung Chu?
faqs.a: According to Mongabay India, after three years of agitation the Dzumsa of Lachung decided in 2009 to ban hydropower projects on its rivers, and proposing one in public is treated as an offence in the village. That decision, taken by a traditional council, has kept the Lachung Chu free of large dams.

faqs.q: Who are the Lachungpa and Lachenpa?
faqs.a: They are the Bhutia communities of Lachung and Lachen, who historically moved between winter homes in the villages and summer pastures higher up with yaks and sheep. Today many also run lodges, drive vehicles and grow apples and potatoes. They speak a Bhutia dialect and follow Tibetan Buddhism, with a monastery in each village.

faqs.q: Can visitors attend a Dzumsa meeting?
faqs.a: Dzumsa meetings are village business and not tourist events, so do not expect to attend. If you are curious, ask your lodge owner or driver about how the village is run; many people are happy to explain over tea. Respect any request not to photograph or record.

faqs.q: Is the Dzumsa found anywhere else in Sikkim?
faqs.a: The Dzumsa as a legally recognised body exists only in Lachen and Lachung. Other villages in Sikkim elect ordinary Gram Panchayats under the state panchayat law. Similar traditional councils exist in other Tibetan Buddhist communities of the Himalaya, but the Sikkim law names only these two.

faqs.q: How can I support the community in Lachung and Lachen?
faqs.a: Stay in locally owned lodges, eat local food, buy apples or other produce from village stalls, hire snow gear in the village, follow the Dzumsa's rules on plastic and rubbish, and tip your driver fairly. Avoid bargaining hard over small sums. Your spending supports the same households who govern the valley.
